summary: Defines a method for supporting GMPLS bidirectional label switched paths where the two directions have different bandwidth. It works with any switching technology and builds on RSVP's model. It moves the experiment in RFC 5467 to the standards track and obsoletes it.

eli5.summary: Most two-way paths have equal capacity both ways, but real needs differ, like fast downloading and slow uploading. This lets GMPLS paths give each direction its own size.

questions: what is an asymmetric bandwidth bidirectional lsp
what is the difference between rfc 5467 and rfc 6387
subtitle: How GMPLS paths can reserve different bandwidth in each direction, using three new RSVP objects.

tldr.problem: GMPLS bidirectional Label Switched Paths could only reserve the same bandwidth in both directions, but some uses, notably MPLS-TP, need different amounts for each direction.
tldr.mechanism: Three new RSVP objects, UPSTREAM_TSPEC, UPSTREAM_ADSPEC and UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC, carry the upstream traffic parameters in the same way the existing objects carry the downstream ones.
tldr.outcome: The approach is the one from the experimental RFC 5467 with no technical changes. It is now on the standards track and RFC 5467 is obsoleted.

today: RFC 6387 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes the experimental RFC 5467. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Asymmetric Bandwidth
sections.content:
GMPLS, as defined in RFC 3473, introduced explicit support for bidirectional Label Switched Paths (LSPs). That support matched switching technologies such as Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) and lambdas, and it only allowed symmetric bandwidth: the same reservation in each direction.

An asymmetric bandwidth bidirectional LSP has a different bandwidth reservation in each direction. The idea was first discussed for Ethernet and published as Experimental in RFC 5467, because it was thought unlikely to be deployed. The MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) requires such LSPs, so this document moves the experiment to the standards track. It states that it has no technical changes from RFC 5467, and it drops the Ethernet-specific alternative from that RFC's appendix, keeping a single approach that works with any technology.
sections.eli5: Old two-way paths always gave both directions the same amount of room. Now some jobs need more room one way than the other, so the rules were upgraded.

sections.title: How RSVP Carries Bandwidth Today
sections.content:
RSVP treats bandwidth parameters as opaque objects. In the original model from RFC 2205, the sender puts SENDER_TSPEC and ADSPEC in Path messages, and the receiver answers with a FLOWSPEC in Resv messages. The SENDER_TSPEC describes what the sender can generate, the FLOWSPEC says what resources should be allocated, and the ADSPEC tells the receiver and intermediate hops what is actually available.

With bidirectional LSPs in RFC 3473 the model changed implicitly. The SENDER_TSPEC indicates the desired resources for both directions, and the FLOWSPEC just confirms what was allocated. The ADSPEC only has meaning for downstream traffic, or is irrelevant.
sections.eli5: Normally the sender asks for room and the receiver says yes. With two-way paths that asking only covered one amount for both ways, so there was no place to ask for two different amounts.

sections.title: The Approach: Mirror Objects for Upstream
sections.content:
The existing SENDER_TSPEC, ADSPEC and FLOWSPEC objects stay as they are and refer only to traffic in the downstream direction. Three new objects are added: UPSTREAM_TSPEC, UPSTREAM_ADSPEC and UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC. They are used exactly like the old ones but describe the upstream flow, and they travel in messages going the opposite way.

The approach is generic and applies to any switching technology supported by GMPLS. It is limited to Point-to-Point (P2P) LSPs; Point-to-Multipoint bidirectional LSPs are not covered.
sections.eli5: There was one form for asking for room. Now there is a second, matching form for the other direction, so each direction can ask for its own amount.

sections.title: Object Procedures
sections.content:
An asymmetric LSP is set up with the bidirectional procedures of RFC 3473 plus the three new objects. Each new object has the same format as its downstream twin.

  • UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC (class number 120): the Path message MUST contain it. Its C-Type MUST match the SENDER_TSPEC C-Type. A node that cannot allocate a label or resources from it MUST send a PathErr with a "Routing problem/MPLS label allocation failure" indication.
  • UPSTREAM_TSPEC (class number 121): describes the traffic that starts at the egress. It MUST be in any Resv message answering a Path that held an UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC, and its contents MAY differ from that object.
  • UPSTREAM_ADSPEC (class number 122): MAY be included in such a Resv message, is processed like an ADSPEC, and MAY be updated or added at transit nodes.

When the ingress receives an UPSTREAM_TSPEC, it MAY decide the original reservation is not enough. It can then tear the LSP down with a PathTear, or send a new Path message with an updated UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC. That change might force a re-route and, in extreme cases, tear the LSP down if resources run out.
sections.eli5: The starting end asks for the amount it wants for the return trip. The far end can say what it actually plans to send back, and if that is more than was reserved, the start can ask again or give up.

sections.title: Message Formats
sections.content:
The new objects appear in specific RSVP messages. UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC goes with the sender descriptor in Path, PathTear, PathErr and Notify. UPSTREAM_TSPEC and UPSTREAM_ADSPEC go with the flow descriptor list in Resv, ResvConf, ResvTear, ResvErr and Notify.

In the sender descriptor, <UPSTREAM_LABEL> and <UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC> are required after the optional objects. In the flow descriptors, <UPSTREAM_TSPEC> follows the <FLOWSPEC> and an optional <UPSTREAM_ADSPEC> may follow it. The syntax follows RFC 5511, and unmodified formats are not repeated.
sections.eli5: This part is the exact checklist of which forms go into which kinds of letters, so every router reads them in the same order.

sections.title: Compatibility With Older Nodes
sections.content:
The three new objects use class numbers of the form 0bbbbbbb. Under RFC 2205, a node that does not support this extension will not recognize those class numbers and responds with an "Unknown Object Class" error. The error propagates to the ingress, which can then avoid the incompatible node or simply end the session.

IANA assigned the classes in the RSVP PARAMETERS registry: 120 for UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC (same C-Types as FLOWSPEC, C-Num 9), 121 for UPSTREAM_TSPEC (same as SENDER_TSPEC, C-Num 12) and 122 for UPSTREAM_ADSPEC (same as ADSPEC, C-Num 13).
sections.eli5: If a router has never heard of the new forms, it says so, and the sender can pick a route around it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The new objects parallel the old ones but are used in the opposite direction. So any vulnerability that comes from the old objects now applies to messages flowing in the reverse direction.

The document adds no new signaling messages and does not change the relationship between control-plane neighbors, so it adds no further message- or neighbor-related concerns. It points to RFC 3473 and RFC 5920 for the wider discussion of GMPLS and RSVP-TE security.
sections.eli5: The new forms can be misused in the same ways as the old ones, just going the other way. Nothing brand new is added to worry about.
